To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a single-photon, time-gated imaging system can be used for in vivo fluorescence lifetime imaging, (ii) the phasor representation is a useful tool to analyze the lifetime of a fluorophore when the decay is broadened, (iii) a single-phosphor-based lifetime imaging system can detect few hundred thousand cells through highly scattering media.

we have developed a new method of FLI through highly scattering media that is based on the use of a time-gated SPAD camera with the phasor analysis, and that we have successfully demonstrated this method for in vivo imaging of cells in a phantom.

the phasors of the fluorescence decays of cells and tissues are well separated in the phasor space, and that the phasoral distribution is broadened with increasing light scattering, and can be used to extract the lifetime of a fluorophore in highly scattering medium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a novel time-gated, single-photon, phasor-based FLI system for in vivo imaging through scattering tissues.
the use of the SPAD-based phasor method for time-gated FLI through highly scattering media.
the development of a novel time-gated SPAD imager, Swiss SPAD2, and its application to fluorescence lifetime imaging through highly scattering medium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the phasors of the SwissSPAD2 can be used as a tool for lifetime imaging in highly scattering media.
our approach can be used for FLI in vivo, but only when fluorescence intensity is high enough to overcome the AF and the broadening of the fluorescence lifetime.

, in vivo, the lifetime of a fluorophore can be measured through scattering medium, provided that the signal level is higher than the AF and that the decay broadening does not result in a complete overlapping of the phasor clouds of the fluorophores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phasors of single fluorophores can still be distinguished even when the fluorescence signal is significantly reduced due to scattering and AF, as long as it is higher than the background noise.
, with the use of a SPAD imager and a wide-field microscope, we can detect a few hundred thousand cells expressing a fluorescent protein in a highly scattering phantom layer.
the use of a time-gated SPAD imager and the phasor-based FLI approach allows for the detection of fluorescence lifetime through highly scattering medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
time-gated FLI can provide a robust, high-resolution, and high-sensitivity tool for imaging of fluorescently labelled cells and tissues in vivo.

, by using a time-gated SPAD imager with an appropriate acquisition time, it is possible to perform FLI through highly scattering medium with single-photon sensitivity, and that the phasors provide a fast, simple and robust tool for lifetime imaging.

, by using a wide-field SPAD imager with short acquisition time and phasor analysis, FLI can be used to study biological samples in vivo through scattering media, with minimal impact of the scattering on the lifetime measurements.
